episode_title: The Power of Expressive Grounding: Using Art to Navigate Overwhelm with Sydney Fowler

real_qa.q: What does expressive grounding mean and how can it help people manage overwhelm?
real_qa.r: Expressive grounding is utilizing creativity and intelligence to ground yourself with your emotions through simple artistic activities like coloring or singing without needing to define or explain what you are doing. You can express and pour out emotions without analyzing where they come from, allowing you to recenter yourself and gently care for yourself so you can continue through the day. You can't always attend a therapy session, but you can take care of yourself in a moment, doing a little bit at a time.

real_qa.q: What are the early warning signs that someone is experiencing emotional clutter and overwhelm?
real_qa.r: The first signs are when breathing speeds up or when you get short with other people. If you notice these patterns starting at your place of work or home, those are very clear signs you might need to step back and think about yourself more than your outside world, because you can only love someone as much as you love yourself.

real_qa.q: How can people use creativity to express things that are difficult to put into words?
real_qa.r: There is a universal language we all have, and we respond to certain colors and sounds at certain frequencies. Take a moment to figure out what you are drawn to, and that will tell you more about yourself after the fact. By opening yourself up to things you are not yet aware are already in you—things that are the same in every other person—you can express feelings without words through responses to colors and emotional resonance that everybody shares differently based on their own journey.

real_qa.q: What simple expressive grounding exercise can someone do immediately when feeling overwhelmed?
real_qa.r: Close your eyes and inhale deeply through your nose into your diaphragm, lifting your shoulders to feel the tension, then exhale through your mouth and bring your shoulders down, releasing everything. Do this three to five times while imagining positivity and light entering and negativity leaving. Then lift your arms above your head as high as they will go and stretch, feeling blood flow through your body and getting oxygen to as much of your body as you can. The very first thing you can do is focus on your breath.

real_qa.q: How can finding your local community theater help you reconnect with your identity and work through personal problems?
real_qa.r: By attending a live theater performance, you can recognize yourself or people you know in the characters on stage and actively work through your own problems. Sydney found that everything she was going through in her life was true of characters she played, and running through how she would choose to do something versus how the character did it was huge for working out her own problems and seeing how someone else handles similar situations, then making choices based on wisdom from what she observed.

guest.bio_context: Sydney Fowler is a South Carolina-based multidisciplinary artist with a Bachelor of Arts degree exploring performance, stage management, directing, drawing, and spoken word. She overcame a significant speech impediment by pursuing theater intensely for 10 years, participating in at least four productions annually. She recently spoke at the Powerful on Purpose Summit with Dr. Tabitha Russell, a pivotal moment where she integrated all her creative work into a personal platform.

real_quote: It's for people who don't realize their artistry as much as it's for people who have practiced their artistry. It asks you just to take a moment and explore a part of you that resides in you and is probably just a little dormant.
